product_title: Reliance Products Aqua-Pak 2.5 Gallon Rigid Water Container
review_headline: Poor design on spout and vent hole.
review_body:
First off, the good:
The bottle is well constructed and seals nicely for travel. No leaks! Very solid design.

Now for the bad:
The spout opening is fairly large. I bought this to refill your standard 2 liter water bottles (Aqua Fina or Dasani or the like) (cap size and opening is pretty standard across most soft drink and water bottles. Since the spout's opening is larger than a standard bottle it ends up dumping most of the water all over the bottle rather than being able to fill it nicely. It would have been nice for the spout to be tapered to fit within bottles to avoid this problem.

The really bad:
The vent hole is plugged with a peg that took a pair of pliers to remove. The plastic of the bottle is so thick that the little peg has to be jammed in very deep to get a good seal. That being said, it needs a lot of force to remove it and to reinsert it each time. And the peg is so small it's easily misplaced. A better design would be a vent plug that is can be popped out to let air in but still remain part of the bottle.

product_title: The North Face Surge II Daypack - TNF Black
review_headline: After over 20 not quite right backpacks and messenger bags...the search is over
review_body:
As senior professoinal engineer and advid outdoor enthusiast I wanted one backpack for all occastions. I've had been using the timbuk2 messenger bag for a while, but it really only carried my work gear. I wanted a bag that could carry my laptop, ipad, cords chargers, external hard drive, flash drives, cameras, sunglasses, lunch, extra clothes, rain jacket, water bottle, and many other miscellanous things...and not look to bulky and maintain a professoinal look. This is it. What sets this bag apart from all the others (even had a north face recon backpack) is every compartment is functional. The build quality is exceptional. The zippers are high quality metal and work smartly. Fully loaded the weight inside distributes itself very evenly thanks to the compartments and how they are organized. everything is centered and makes for ease of carrying. The straps are one of the most comfortable straps I've worn with a shock absorbing material inside the finds the perfect balance between not being too stiff or to rubbery. Padding in the laptop compartment is well thought out to proect the most susceptable hit points of your laptop (corners and bottom).

Pros:
*Im able to fit my lunch bag in the middle compartment and have enough a spare set of clothes.
http://www.amazon.com/eBags-Slim-Lunch-Box-Titanium/dp/B0013KIIZU/ref=sr_1_76?s=kitchen&ie=UTF8&qid=1427906282&sr=1-76
is the perfect lunch bag for this pack.

*There is seperate storage for laptop and ipad. With a 13" macbook air I am not challenging the space provided and could see a 17" laptop fitting in the provided compartment. I also like the 3/4 length zipper of the laptop compartment. This helps prevent the uncontrolled falling out of your laptop.

*The sunglass holder is lined with a velvet like material that resisits scratching of the shades. It's easily accessible.

* The middle compartment is huge and with the compression straps fully extended.

*The office compartment (most outer compartment) carries most of my electronic accessories. There is a nice large mesh pocket at the top that is perfect for my lapto charger. No more digging around the bottom of my backpack and pulling many items on top just to charge my laptop.

*The two outer pockets are seperate pockets. The zippers are beefier here and provide quick and reliable access to these spaces.

*There is one water bottle holder on the side. It fairly deep and fits standard water bottles as well as my larger nalgene 32oz bottle.

* The molle loops on the back are nice and conveinent for attaching my keys to quickly.

*The nylon fabric (up to 1680D) is extremely durable.

review_body: I purchased this rack and had a friend help me put it together.  It is easy to put together but it took us a little longer to install because we didn't follow the instructions where it states that you should put your bike on the rack to adjust where to put the tire brackets.  You also need to put the bike on the installed rack so that you can adjust where it sits in relation to the back of your car otherwise it may sit off center.  I was able to drive into my garage with the rack on my car.  The Sport Rider 2 rack is built solidly and worked well for transporting my bike.  I did use a Velcro strap where the hook attaches to the bike's top tube to secure it more tightly for extra insurance.  I also ordered the Fat Tire Adapter Kit for the rack from eTrailer.com (Part # HRSPRWH-F) and they fit perfectly.  The bike rack is easy to install on your car.  I'm a woman and I could do it easily as it weighs no more than 40 lbs.  This is my first bike rack but I think it's a good rack for the money.

product_title: Aqua Lung Shot FX Spring Strap Diving Fin
review_headline: Highly Recommended - Powerful, Efficient, and no Knee Pain!
review_body: I purchased these fins for a Feb/March 2015 trip to Raja Ampat and around the Philippines. I am a cold water diver, and I typically wear Tusa Splits to alleviate the knee pain that was occurring when I wore paddle fins. However, splits are not the best for currents, and I knew that Raja Ampat would be more current intensive that my usual diving. Based on reviews, I purchased the Aqualung Shot FX. I was a little worried that they would bother my knees, but I am happy to report that I didn't get a flinch of knee pain during the 30+ dives I wore them. I LOVE these fins. They are powerful, I can keep up with my fast husband, and I can frog kick efficiently in these. I received so many compliments on them as well. My husband was curious, so he wore them for the one dive I skipped due to sinus pressure, and he was very impressed. I'm looking forward to trying these out with my cold water gear setup, and I expect to sell my other fins and use these full time instead. I highly recommend the Aqualung Shot FX!

product_title: Guardian Accessories Pocket Knife Survival Multitool W Compass [10 Tools]
review_headline: Mostly junk.  Spend the extra money on a Victorinox SwissCard.  You'll use it more often and be a happier camper.
review_body: Edit 4/13/2015 I just tried to use the "cute" can opener.  Like the rest of this tool, it's completely worthless.  In order for a jack-knife type can opener to work you need leverage.  The total length of the can opener in this tool is 1.5 inches.  The "handle" has a flat-tip screwdriver blade on the bottom.  In effect, it forces a screwdriver into the pad of your index finger if you attempt to use it.  Even with leather gloves on, there's not enough leverage to even put a dent in the top of a can of tuna.  -- original post -- The compass has an air bubble inside that makes it difficult if not impossible to get a true reading.  The bubble sticks to the dial and the needle moves around if you tilt the card slightly.  You can only know if the reading is correct if you already know which way is North. But if you already know that, then you don't need a compass...  The plastic tweezers are too flimsy to be useful in removing a splinter.  The blades bend so easily that they won't close if they're touching your skin.  If you hold the magnifying glass less than 3/8 of an inch from a surface the card creates a shadow and you can't see what you're trying to look at.  If you hold the magnifying glass more than 3/8 of an inch above the surface, it flips the image upside down.  So if you're trying to use the magnifier to remove a splinter, forget it.  The blade is sharp enough out of the box to be useful for cutting, but it has more cons than pros.  The cutout at the lower rear of the knife blade looks cool but is only useful if you want to use the knife as a stabbing weapon.  In order to actually cut something you need to pinch the blade in front of the plastic handle.  The short length of the blade means that you can't get much leverage when cutting.  The wrench slots in the blade also look cool but, due to the short length of the blade, you can't get much leverage.  If your hand slips while putting torque on the blade to loosen or tighten a nut/bold, you havea 50/50 chance of slicing your fingers.  Like I said, the blade is sharp enough out of the box to be useful.  Though I don't recommend using it to intentionally slice yourself.  The only two features that I can find no fault with are the toothpick and the can-bottle opener/screw driver combo.  The can-bottle opener/dual screw driver is actually well designed and might make its way into a bug-out kit.  The rest of the card will go into my drawer of wasted time and money.  I recommend paying the extra quality for a Victorinox SwissCard.  I've owned one for 10 years and have used every tool it offers without fail.  It's well designed, well made, and as long as your girlfriend doesn't try to use the ink pen to pry open a tea tin, it'll last a lifetime.

product_title: ALPS Mountaineering Tri-Leg Stool, Rust
review_headline: surprisingly comfy even for someone that likes luxury camp chairs
review_body:
I've always liked the fancier camp chairs, with the perspective of "the more cup holders, tables, footrests and adjustability, the better.". Well, my son did not inherit those genes from me. He is a minimalist, and requested a stool to replace a perfectly fine bag chair. Since these were moderately priced, I agreed to let him try one. To my surprise, he is ecstatic, and I am impressed.

- Folds up easily
- Has an attached shoulder strap on the stool, so it can be carried even without using the bag.
- Has a keeper strap like an umbrella to gather up the seat fabric neatly and keep it together.
- When seated, your rear will be about 14 inches off the ground. Perfect for shorter to average height people, those that are taller will likely have their knees higher than parallel when seated
- Those that need assistance to push off to stand from low sofas would not do well with this
- Lack of cupholders not an issue, as you can easily reach the ground
- Your weight is balanced so it encourages proper posture, making it more comfy to sit on than just a wooden stool, for example
- Super light, and will fit into his Scout camping footlocker (Contico wheeled tote) to keep his gear consolidated

product_title: Primus ETA Express Spider Stove
review_headline: Powerful, efficient, flexible.  what's not to like?
review_body:
The Primus ETA Spider is a wonderfully over-engineered hybrid of multiple Primus technologies all rolled into one.

It has the stand alone stove flexibility of a backpacking liquid fuel stove, it has the wind-screen protection of the ETA Power EF/MF series, and uses the incredibly versatile lindal valve fuel line and highly reliable ergopump.

The real magic of the ETA Power EF and this stove, the ETA Spider, is simmer control, and low heat efficiency. With most other stoves, high heat output efficiency is the goal, so they are highly efficient at boiling water fast. But with the ETA stoves, you can throttle heat back to a fairly low level, which allows slower cooking, or boiling water with less fuel. Everything about the ETA series is focused on extending the life of fuel, and the difference is significant.

Just one example: Both the ETA Power EF and the ETA Spider come with a thermal insulated bag or cozy, which further improves efficiency. When cooking stews, pastas in thick sauces, curry, and the like, you can cook the food to 80-90% and then turn the stove off, place the pot in the cozy, and let it finish cooking.

All three stoves in the ETA line have very special features that combine efficiency and flexibility, but of the three, the ETA Spider wins the prize in flexibility.

-----
A quick word about the other ETA stoves:

With a 1.8L pot and grooves designed for the 3L pot, the ETA Power EF is the big daddy of the family, and while its efficiency can't be denied, the stove is a part of the wind screen and can't be used independantly of it. The wind screen contains the pot stand as well, further limiting flexibility. This limits the stove's usability, as using frying pans or additional sauce pans becomes a bit of a challenge.

The ETA Lite, while containing several well engineered components and a unique triangular locking mechanism, has the same limitations of most stoves that are lock-stacked above the gas canister.

----

The ETA Spider, the newest addition to the ETA family, adds even greater flexibility. Really, the core stove portion looks similar to many portable stoves today in that there are three legs which are all folded together and also doubles as the pot stand, and then there is a fuel line to connect to a fuel source (gas canister or liquid fuel bottle). This means that the stove can be used without the windscreen.

The windscreen has three magnets at the base that align with the stove legs to keep the stove stable, almost as stable as the ETA Power EF.

The pot stand portion of the legs come just a hair above the edge of the windscreen, so you can really use any pot/pan/cup you like on the stove. You're not limited to what you use. And therein lies the key differentiator between the ETA Spider and the ETA Power EF. With the EF, you can use other pots, but it is cumbersome because the pot holder pieces are recessed under the rim of the of the windscreen, and you can't use the stove without the windscreen.

Moving on the the pot (or sauce pan, if you will):

The pot has fold out handles that hug the pot when folded in, and this then fits in the windscreen. It's a tight fit, but fits just fine.

The pot itself has a non-stick coating, and while this is much thicker than most non-stick coatings I've seen on backpacking gear, it's no where near the thickness in coating of a kitchen pan, so burn in will eventually occur. Still, the coating is noticeably thicker than than the non-stick coatings on most backpacking sets I own, so with care, burn-in could be delayed for a pretty long time. Just remember, the ETA series of stoves are very heat efficient, so keep the heat output low, and the coating could last a long time.

The ETA Spider also comes with a food bowl (Just like the ETA Power EF). I typically use that during food prep, as I like topre-cook some ingredients before throwing everything together into whatever stew-like or pasta'ish or curry'like concoction being prepared, but if you have the efficiency to prepare everything in the pot and cook in phases, it'd still be fine being used for it's intended purpose, a food bowl.

In a simple test, I boiled a little over half a liter in 2:40. Really it was boiling at about 2:20, But I don't count water as boiling until the water is at its most aggressive rolling boil.

Of course, the great thing about this set is that you can purchase, separately, the multi-fuel kit, which allows you to use white gas, kerosene, and other similar fuels (No alcohol though). This is particularly useful if you're not sure what fuel you'll have and want some flexibility, or if you are trying to avoid the trash buildup of empty gas canisters, or if you are planning on cookng in particular cold weather and want a more stable and consistent fuel in dramatically changing temperature conditions.

A small tip: Primus sells several multi-fuel kits, for the older Gravity stove, the ETA Power EF/MF/SPider, but the kits are all essentially identical, only very different prices. The ETA Spider multi-fuel kit sells for over $100, the Gravity multi-fuel kit sells for $55. They're all the same. The ETA Power EF kit sells for $75, I think. There is one small differece. The spider multifuel kit comes with a separate plate. The ETA Power EF has the heating plate built into the stove, but the ETA Spider doesn't. The heating plate is where you put a little of the fuel to pre-heat the copper rigid fuel ingress point. This heats the fuel enough to catch and at least get flame out of the stove, and that flame coming out of the stove then heats the generator, making the fuel vaporize more efficiently. But, i just fashion a small bowl out of aluminum foil.

Interestingly, Primus now also sells the ETA Spider without the wind screen and pot, so you can just get the stove portion. I'm not sure why anyone would do this because the stove has one small flaw, well, not a flaw so much as a slightly fragile design:

Many liquid fuel capable stoves on the market today and many older backpacking stoves all need some way to pre-heat the fuel to vaporize it. In days past, it was done through something called a "generator" or "heat coil" or "heating element". All this really means is that the fuel line didn't go directly into the stove. Rather, the fuel line connects to a brass tube that goes around the top of the stove to be pre-heated and vaporized before coming back around to send fuel into the stove fuel injection point.

This is particularly true of Kerosene/diesel/parafin as the vaporization temperature is very high (which is also what makes it such a safe fuel), but applies to white gas and petrol as well (which has a lower flash point, and is therefore less safe, but also easier to deal with). This is true of gas cansiter stoves including butane stoves as well, it's just less noticeable because the temperature where it needs pre-heating is so low, that under most 3 season camping conditions, it doesn't need pre-heating.

That generator typically is made of brass because brass isn't as affected by heat as other metals. However, while brass is very strong in resistance to temperature, it's very weak as a structural metal. Brass is soft. And unfortunately, since it needs to be above the flame, it needs to be completely exposed....soft metal...completely exposed...equals fragile.

It was a genius design back in the day (though generators were always on any purchasable spare parts list), but if you look at the Primus Omnifuel/Omnilite, Optimus Nova+/Polaris Optifuel (I own and use all of these marvels), you'll see that the best engineering today gets rid off this weak link in backpacking stoves, instead building the pre-heating element into a short, hardened straight line tube, which draws heat not from the stove fire, but from the entire copper assembly, including the soot trap. Which is why it's interesting that the ETA series, the pinnacle of Primus stove engineering, uses this older technology.

Except for that one issue, which is less worrying since the stove assembly is always stored in the ETA Spider pot itself, the Primus ETA Spider is among the best stove setups I own.u can just get the stove portion. product_title: XLAB Torpedo System 100 with Composite VEE Cage & Alloy Mount
review_body:
I'm quite pleased with the Torpedo and it functions exactly as designed, although the mount and bottle cage aren't much to look at. A training partner has the Torpedo 400 with the carbon fiber cage, which costs twice the price. I'd be on the fence to "upgrade" if I ever need to replace this one, the function is the same, with a slight weight advantage, so it's really just aesthetics for me - a lot to pay for aesthetics.

The computer mount is surprisingly stable. As an engineer myself, when I looked at the mounting system for the bottle chassis, and noted the computer mount's hanging position out front, I expected it to bounce and shake on the road, but to my surprise and to my pleasure, it's been very stable on the road.

The provided bite tip tube works well, but when it came time to replace it, I used med grade tubing and a camelback bite tip. I did add a piece of latex rubber under the refillable lid to help top the little amount of spilling that happened on fast turns or bigger bumps. Refill works well, and is in a much easier location than a frame mounted refillable bottle.

I'm riding a Specialized Shiv with the formed aluminum cockpit. The mount rides tight between the extensions, and puts my Garmin perfectly between my thumbs for easy reach to the buttons, and directly in my eyeline without bowing my head too far (like a stem mount). I tried the new Xlab garmin mount that rides on top of the bottle, but found that I prefer the forward mount. The bottle is shielded from the front by my hands, and it's invisible from the side, shielded between my forearms.

product_title: Peak Design Leash
review_body:
My favorite strap, ever. I use it with my Panasonic GX7 m43 camera, and a Canon SX50 superzoom. I am big and tall (6'4 and 280 lb) and the strap is more than long enough to wear across the body, sling style. The slim strap is comfortable for a whole afternoon carrying loads up to the 45-150mm on the GX7, which is the heaviest combo I currently shoot.

The slick nylon of this strap has two big benefits: it allows the strap to slide and settle over clothes without grabbing them and bunching them up. This is both better for appearances, and allows the strap to better distribute the load making it more comfortable than I expected given its thinness. And most importantly, it allows the strap to slide easily and function like a sling, without extra hardware or the need to hang the camera upside down like with many sling carriers.

The plastic hardware is quiet and less likely to catch on clothes. And the quick release clips are very convenient when I want to mount the camera on a scope and not have strap dangling and getting in the way.

Highly recommended!

product_title: Klarus P1A XP-G R5 Cree LED Flashlight, Grey
review_headline: P1A is punching above it's weight class!!
review_body: I've owned a lot of highend flashlights from all the big brands. This little light is amazingly well made. The tail switch feels good. It has square threads, and an orange peel reflector.The knurling is superbly executed, and actually offers grip. Of all the "Chinese high performance light brands", Klarus has become one of my favorites.  This little light is IPX-8 waterproof, and submersible. It is also rated to be dropped from 1.5 meters, which is awesome for any light to meet that standard. There are brighter lights with more bell and whistles, but they aren't higher quality then the Klarus Professional Series. I have served in combat in the Middle East, and I can tell you, you want simplicity in a tactical light, and this light "fits the bill" extremely well. This would make an excellent flashlight for E.D.C.\self defense. Don't underestimate this budget light.

And I noticed that more threads are giving away along the seams of the legs on the outside below the knees. I discovered Senior Blend several years ago and I'm fairly certain it brought our beloved Aussie back from a few, inexplicable "near-death" episodes. Vet tests would prove inconclusive but her energy levels would plummet. She would act like she was a day from death. I'd give her Senior Blend for a week or so and that dog would come back even stronger than before. It became our inside joke that she'd outlive us all while on Senior Blend.

She died a few weeks ago at a few months shy of 16. Her body was still very strong but she developed dementia and her night terrors became horrendous. We made the impossible choice of euthanizing her because she was truly suffering almost every night.

We will always be profoundly grateful to the makers of Senior Blend for helping our baby live such a long and healthy life.

product_title: Timbuk2 Command Laptop Travel-Friendly Messenger Bag
review_headline: An excellent bag one year in
review_body:
I've used this bag for over a year, and it's absolutely fantastic for my needs as a professor who occasionally travels to conferences.

For daily use, I usually carry my MacBook Air and its charger, my iPad mini, any papers I need, one text book, my lunch, and all of the other briefcase-like items that accumulate (pen case, phone cable and charger, etc). It's been great for this use, and I don't need to use any additional sleeves to provide padding for the laptop or iPad.

I love not having to take my laptop out for airport security, although I do need to move the iPad into the main pocket since you cannot stack a tablet and a laptop when going through security. But, I immediately move it back into its slot right after I put my shoes and belt back on.

I still find the latches a little weird, but I've gotten used to them. One slight downside is that if the bag is full and I pick it up by the handle (not the shoulder strap), then the straps do loosen a bit. But that's minor nitpicking.

This is my first Timbuk2 product, and based on the first year, I expect it to last me a long, long time. I won't hesitate to replace it with another one in the future.

review_headline: Highly recommended--give time to fully charge
review_body:
I have 3 WakaWakas. I use them, one at a time, as night lights in a bathroom with only one electrical outlet. I need more light in the bathroom at night. So . . . I keep three WakaWakas charging during the day by placing them in a vertical position on a south facing windowsill. In Maine, not every day is sunny but with three WakaWakas I am able to stay ahead of the clouds. I can also recharge the devices by putting them under a low wattage incandescent bulbs. An LED will not recharge the device. I haven't tried to charge it from the light of a CFL.

When the WakaWaka is turn to the lowest setting, it lasts all night and is still operating in the morning--usually a period of 9-10 hours. They're useful at camp where we have only gas lights. Highly recommended. Just be patient and give a chance to fully charge.

product_title: Scuba Choice Scuba Diving BCD Standard Male BC to Male 1/4 NPT Adaptor
review_body: Had no idea this sort of adapter existed until I spoke with someone on a dive boat. This adapter connects to your LP house in place of a BCD inflator and threads to standard 1/4in NPT connectors found on air tools and hoses. I used this with a HOG D3 first stage, 30ft of cheap hose and a harbor freight budget impact and easily took off my vehicle's flywheel bolts which were 1/2in torqued to 105ft/lbs and glued in. Tried for 45 minutes with opposing wrenches and couldnt get one to budge, but the impact worked great.  I am assuming any decent SCUBA regulator will put out the psi and cfm to run almost any standard air tool and the fitting didn't seem to hinder performance. Make sure you get the correct connector for your LP BCD quick disconnect as some brands of BCDs have different styles of connections. I bought 2 just to have one with my air tools and one with my SCUBA stuff, just in case.  The photos show how I connected the adapter to the BCD LP disconnect/1/4in NPT disconnect.  The whole system with regulator.  The bag with foam padding (mailed inside a padded envelope). A close up of the connector itself, removed from packaging.

product_title: Igloo Iceless Thermoelectric Cooler
review_headline: It works exactly as the manual says - I like it. Whoo-hoo!
review_body: This cooler was exactly what I expected.  First off, what I measured; Current draw at 13.5 Volts was about 4.7 Amperes. At 12.2 Volts the current draw was about 3.5 Amperes. The manual says 3.5 to 4.8 Amperes, The manual agrees with my measurements.  Secondly, this is a thermoelectric cooler.  It uses about 40 - 60 Watts of energy so it will not cool down a load of warm soda in a few hours. The manual recommends running this for a few hours prior to adding your material. If you put warm sodas in this, expect to wait 20-25 (or more) hours for them to get cold. If you put in cold sodas, this will keep them very cold while running.  Regarding the cord heating problems that others have stated. I connected this to a 'motorcycle' DC receptacle that I had purchased years ago. My receptacle got quite warm while this cooler was running. This was not a problem with the cooler's plug. It was my receptacle not being able to handle the current draw. If you have a good quality receptacle, this device will work good, without heat problems. My plug did not get hot or melt. If you have a worn receptacle it could get hot.  The plug on this device has a built in (removable) 7.5 Ampere fuse. I would not recommend running this with on a vehicle with the motor off as it would probably run your battery down in after a few hours, there is no low voltage shut off built in.

product_title: Schwinn Gridlock Men's comfort bike (26-Inch)
review_headline: All my bikes have been schwinn except for my electric bike.
review_body: I started out with a Schwinn at 7 years of age and I am now 70 years old. I love this bike and I have put 300 miles on it. The gears shift easily and I like the fact that each set of gears (three directly on the pedals and 7 on the rear axle) have individual gear shift levers on each side of the handle bar. The gear numbers are easily read through a small window on each gear changer device. I like the old style handle bars at my age ; they take the strain off of my arms and neck. It allows to set more upright. One selector goes from 1-3 and the other goes from 1-7. I have notice when I am in low or "1" on the 1-3 gear changer I don't use "7" on the other gear changer as well as when I am in "3" on the 1-3 changer I don't use "1" on the 1-7 changer. The reason for this is , you are forcing the chain to cross from one side of the axle gearing to the extreme other side of the pedal gearing. This will wear your chain and sprockets out faster. I highly recommend this bike especially for the older crowd !!

product_title: Continental SuperSport Plus Urban Bicycle Tire
review_body:
I have an older and weathered 24 speed road bike that still rides well (Treks seem to last). I had purchased this tire from my local bike shop after getting a flat on by back tire and noticing how bad it was cracked.

I was looking into the gator skin line, but they did not have them in in 25mm. I like having the 2-3 mm thicker because it's more comfortable on turns. This tire may weigh every so slightly more than the gator skin, yet rides very well.

I ride in the urban decay of Los Angeles, where tires have caught road debris and I've gotten flats. Not with these. I've had this tire on by back wheel about 130 miles before giving into buying this for my front wheel. Now that I have both wheels with these tires, it rides even better, offering a great combo of traction and some tread. Because of the lack of weather changes, I can only speak for spring and summer riding conditions. I have rode in the rain a couple of times, no problem; but judging by the small treads on the side/wall, I would imagine there are better tires for all season conditions.

Maybe every 50-100 miles they'll need to be checked for cracks and tread before riding. With these Super Sports, all I need to to is check air pressure, because I like to ride the max 120 psi and I've sometimes gone a pump or two over and still rides great.

Bottom line, for a set of road tires, priced under $70, for summer urban/city riding, these are great tires.

review_headline: Hard to control, repairs require shipping to China.
review_body:
At first I was excited for this flashlight, but it broke after a few months. My main complaints are: Clunky brightness changing mechanism, clunky recharging position, terrible customer service.

First off, returning this for repairs will require you to ship the light back to China, which (surprise) costs more than the price of the flashlight! If you view their main site, they have a terrible translator which makes it difficult to read.

The charging mechanism requires you to unscrew the protruding section in the middle of the flashlight, kinda hard to see, but its not easily noticeable at first glance.

The brightness switching mechanism works by loosening the middle of the flashlight (whaaat?) if you tighten the middle, it goes to full brightness, if you loosen, it will switch back to the lower setting. product_title: Kammok Roo Double Camping Hammock
review_body:
Kammok started on Kickstarter in 2011 with the Roo as their first product, and they started strong. When you lay in it there is plenty of room, and it doesn't bind you up or confine you. The material is very soft and dries quickly. I have often gotten out of the ocean or river and hopped right into my hammock. Sleeping in it is easy and comfortable. There may be some lighter options out there, but for me it is worth it. The diamond ripstop is extremely strong. While this hammock is rated for 500 lbs, the material and Kanga Claw carabiners could easily handle more than that. The hammock is 67" wide, so you could put two people in here, but I have never really found that to be comfortable in any hammock. It is a little more expensive than its main competition, but it is worth it for the quality and comfort. Grab a set of python straps and you have a great set up that weight right around 2 lbs. Kammok now makes a bug net and rain tarp to go along with the Roo. I have not tried them yet, but they are out their if you are looking for a complete hammock rig.

Kammok also offers a limited lifetime warranty and recycles its old hammocks, which I like from a company. They also give a percentage of their profits to environmental charities.

product_title: Vilano Tuono Performance Hybrid Flat Bar Commuter Road Bike (700c, 21 Speed Shimano) - 58 cm
review_headline: You Get What You Pay For (or maybe not)
review_body:
Update... 22-Mar-2015
I decided to return this bike. It just had too many problems, starting with the bent fork dropouts on delivery. The biggest problem was the pricing misrepresentation (see original post below). I just could not justify owning it, and trying to upgrade it to what I had expected to get.

I've bought a lot of stuff on Amazon, and this is the 1st Item that I've returned. I'm impressed with how easy it was.

I ended up getting a "used" warehouse deal bike that really was priced a <50% of its value.

I forgot to mention the Direct-Pull Cantilever "V-Brakes" on this bike in my original review. They are (like everything else) cheaply made, but workable (for a while anyway). The brake mechanism itself is sturdy enough, and will properly stop the bike. The levers are OK. The barrel adjuster on the brake lever is exceptionally poor quality in my view. Like everything else, the basic stuff you need is there, it is just poor quality, and will probably not last.

My initial opinion still holds:
This is a throw-away bike, not an investment.

Original Post ... March 11, 2015
Ouch!

This bike screams "Cheap". I gave it 2 stars largely because of the price advertising scheme, which is really a gimmick. This was advertised as a $600 bike, on sale for $300. This is at its absolute very best a marginal deal at $300. I'm sorely disappointed at what I got, compared to what I expected to see, but not enough so to go through the hassle to return it. I'll take my lumps, chalk it up to experience, and give it a go. (After I put some miles on it and put it through the paces, I'll follow-up here with how it actually rides over time.) If you want a cheap bike that looks OK but will not be a likely target by thieves, then you may be in luck here.

The most glaring problem before I even opened the box was that the first time I picked up the carton and set it down I detected that part of the frame was resting directly on the ground. Sure enough, when I pulled the bike assembly out of the box the tips of the (steel) fork were so badly bent I could not get the front wheel on. There were bits of plastic everywhere inside the box, so I'm guessing that they were what was left of what had been inserted into the fork wheel mount as a packing device. It was woefully inadequate. A block of wood and some bolts may have done the trick, but NOT what was supplied. I have enough tools and mechanical experience (and strength) that I was able to muscle the fork tip enough back into place to get the wheel on. It is not perfect, but it fits. I wonder now how much physical damage was done to the steel, which is probably low-grade, and how long before it fails from stress. There was a box inside the carton with the pedals, front wheel clamp, and a few other bits, which had burst open. It does not look like anything is missing (fallen through the holes / gaps in the stressed-out shipping carton). I'll report back later.

The good news is that everything you need to adjust it like a "real' bike is there, it is just all cheaply done, with cheap components. This bike may get you around a bit, but I would not do any serious off-road riding on this thing, it will not likely hold up to the stress. It may hold up for regular commuting on paved surfaces. I intend to ride this bike on a commute of up to 20 miles per day, 3 days a week or more. Most of my route is a paved multi-use "Greenbelt" trail, with one long and steep hill to climb.

The other good news is that despite all its cheapness, this bike is fairly light. It is advertised at 25#, and feels about like that. If I get a more accurate measurement, I'll post it here in a follow-up.

I rate this as a "throw away" bike, not a lifetime investment (like my last two bikes.) Hard times forced me to make this on-line choice, and while I'm OK to live with it for now, I'm betting that I will likely regret it over time. If this bike lasts over 3 to 5 years without a failure that will prompt another purchase, I'll be surprised. For an extra $200 I could have gotten everything I wanted at a local bike shop, which is what I'll do next time. I'll never buy a bike sight-unseen again.

I had clues that this bike was not going to meet my expectations (based on the pricing gimmick), but I ignored them. That is my fault, and I accept that. One major shortcoming was the lack of detailed information on components at the seller and (especially) the manufacturer. This is probably your best clue that the bike will not match the pricing scheme. If quality components are used throughout, the manufacturer will likely advertise all of them with pride. You'd have to really know your stuff though to make an informed decision, either that or do a lot of research. If you do not have the time and/or skill, just go to a bike shop, otherwise you may get burned by an online purchase with shady pricing schemes like this one.

I saw a number of reviews stating that you can buy upgrade parts to overcome the shortcomings of these cheap bikes (this particular one, and all the others out there). If you do your homework though, you will find that by the time you buy all these upgrades, you will likely have spent enough money that you could have just gotten what you wanted in the first place. I intend to ride this bike till it has a catastrophic failure, or until I get get enough cash to get what I really want (hopefully a 3-5 year time-frame).

I had a few questions that the seller and manufacturer site could not answer... regarding:

The seat-post is a fairly standard 27.2 mm diameter... so if you have a nice micro-adjusting seatpost in that size from another bike, it will fit this one. If you look carefully at the photo (in zoom-mode) you can see that this bike has a super cheap seat mount, to a simple straight-tube seat-post. These are OK. The seat mount is just cheap steal though, prone to rust, etc. Even at my height (6'2"), there is about 2' of post left for a taller rider (as advertised in the sizing chart at the mfg. site). The saddle is predictably cheap, but looks OK. With this cut-rate seat-post however, your choices in a better saddle will be limited, unless you upgrade the post too (and all that can get pretty pricey).

There are mounting points built into the frame for a rear rack, and front and rear fenders. The two rear holes near the dropout are threaded. You can see two of the rack mounts on the seat-stay tube. Near the fork dropout there is one threaded set, and one plain drilled set of holes, so adequate options there. This is a nice touch. There are also tubes or locations with holes for fender mounts (front and rear). As advertised there are mounting points for a water bottle in the frame triangle. I've not tested these mount points yet, but will follow-up when I finish installing these accessories.

I'll now describe a few of the major components.

Frame
The frame looks nice, and fairly well made. The paint job is cheap, and chips and flakes easily. As other reviewers stated, it came with scratches that appeared to have been made at the factory (or assembly and packing facility). The front of the head (steering) tube was scuffed up where it had rubbed against the packing box during transit. While it looks like a fairly nice frame, based on everything that follows I have serious doubts as to how well it will hold up with even moderate use.
Note:
Also, one of the control cables (between the head tube and handlebars) had at some point been so badly bent over that it has a permanent crimp in the cable housing, but the cable seems OK (for now).

Wheels
The first thing I learned to look for in a (quality) bike is a one-piece alloy hub, that has a smooth transition from one flange to the other. These wheels have cheap (stamped?) steel hubs, of apparently 3 pieces mashed together (two flanges and a tube separating them). This is one of the first things I saw when I pulled it out of the box that indicated that I'd been had, that this was NEVER a $600 bike.

The rims are a double walled aluminum, as advertised, and seem to be a decent quality. The rim sidewall (braking surface) has very fine concentric grooves milled into it. I've only seen smooth brake walls till now, and these look like a good idea, I’ll report back. The spokes are steel, and look OK.

The rim-band is (cheap) vinyl, and in one spot was poorly aligned and had some wrinkles in it. (I've only checked the front wheel so far.) I already have some (Zefal brand) rim tape to replace or supplement these bands. (I've had good results with this product in the past.) I planned ahead as crummy rim bands are a very common problem (especially on budget bikes), that frequently will lead to a flat. A good, well placed rim-band is essential in ensuring that the tube does not get pinched, poked, or expanded into a cavity (of almost any size), which can eventually result in a flat. I saw enough complaints about this issue in reviews of every bike I looked at in this price range (around $300). (On single walled rims you need to check for spoke ends, that may need filing down.)

There is at least one stray spoke nipple rolling around in the front rim. I doubt it will be an issue, but I’m not too keen on the idea. I probably cannot remove it without completely pulling one of the spoke nipples out. My experience has been that it is best to not mess with a tuned wheel unless you absolutely have to.

The Kenda “KWEST” 700c x 28 tires look pretty decent, and are rated at 50 to 84 psi, which is a nice blend of both firmness and comfort. For the uninitiated, be sure to keep your tire pressure up or you will ding your rim on pot-holes and such, and suffer badly if you have rim brakes.

These use “Presta” (French) valves on the inner-tubes (and my 1st experience w/ ‘em.). Presta valves have long been more popular on serious road bikes than the more common Schrader valves (like on automobile tires). You may need to buy new tire gauges and pumps or attachments (but some can do both). These 700c wheels / tires are sometimes called 29er’s due to the near 29 inch diameter (apparently to the outside tire diameter) but in reality the whole wheel size story can be very confusing. The official diameter on 700c rims is 622 mm, which equals 24.4882 inches. This is actually the “bead seat diameter”, or BSD. Go figure.

These are BIG wheels, and should give you a nice, smooth ride.

Crank Set
The drive sprockets are (cheap) stamped steel, and riveted together. Again, no way this is a $600 bike. (Along with the wheel hubs, this was a major groan-er for me.) The cranks themselves have a cheap finish to them, but look OK. They are “square spindle” style “Prowheel Cold-Forged 6N 170”. (DO NOT attempt to remove these to service the crank bearings without a “crank puller”.) These 170 mm cranks would probably fit someone 5’9” better. At 6’2” plus, I’d probably be better off with a 175+ mm crank, but since I’m not riding all day every day I’ll probably get by. Still, for a bike intended for taller riders (starting at 5’11” on their fitting chart), you’d think they’d outfit it with longer cranks. Yet another cost conflict issue, and an indicator of cheap construction.

Pedals
Whatever they are they are dirt cheap. The reflectors are pressed in with plastic tabs and probably will not last long. On the up-side you can probably mount a “rat-trap” style toe-clip on these, and run a strap through them (which is what I intend to do, as I’m very familiar with that kind of system). The way they are assembled though, it will be a major PITA to get to the bearings in these critters, to check the lubrication or service them. As another reviewer stated, they are really stiff to turn right out of the box, but may loosen up with use. Otherwise, they seem OK, and functional.

Remaining Drive System
The front and rear derailleurs, and the shifters, all look and feel pretty cheap. Time will tell how well they hold up. I’m feeling pretty doubtful right now. I hung the bike up so I could test the operation of the shifting, and the rear derailleur in particular will probably need adjusting, but this is not too uncommon, especially for a brand new bike, and the adjusting screws are easily accessible. The rear sprocket set is a Shimano MF-TZ21 and looks pretty decent. The chain looks adequate. The derailleur control cables run under the crank tube through a flimsy plastic track. Once again, “CHEAP”. This bike is obviously not intended to be a long lasting machine.

Head Tube / Steering
The Stem / Headset are all one piece and non-adjustable. The material is aluminum, and it looks OK, but it has a cheap finish similar to the cranks. I knew this going in, so no surprise, but in light of all the other shortcomings, this is yet another disappointment. (I will find out soon how much of a problem this fixed / low setting will be.) Not a $600 bike by any means. The fork is bound to the frame by a plastic cap underneath the head of the securing bolt. (We’ll see how long that lasts.) The inscription on it indicates “Caged Bearings Inside”. Your call if that is better or worse than loose bearings. In this class bike it probably hardly matters.

All-in-all this is an OK bicycle, that will likely do for light communing, but that is about it. It just does not seem very durable, and is cheaply constructed. The weight is decent, all things considered. I’ll report back on the operation, once I actually get it on the road. This bike may last years, but probably not decades. Consider your investment carefully.

I saw complaints in reviews about the bike being shipped with the bearings being dry. I Intend to try and check the easy ones first, and will report back on what I find.

About me:

I am 6'2", 33-34" inseam, 200#, size 12 shoe. I started out as a Carpenter (for 10 years) and later got a technical degree in engineering. I graduated from high-school in 1976. In the Spring of '76 I bought a new touring bike (a nice one), worked and trained all Summer, and in the Fall took a 1,000 mile bike trek over about one month total for the actual bike trip. I camped as I traveled, so I was fairly loaded down. I did not need a lot of training, as all through HS I frequently did 50 to 100 mile day trips for fun. That Summer was mostly to break-in the new bike. (The absolute best advice I got was: "Bring extra spokes".) All that time, and since then, I've not been shy about stripping a bike down to the ball bearings, cleaning and lubricating, and reassembling. When I was actively riding long distances, I generally did every major bearing set 1x/yr. So: wheel axles, crankset, pedals, steering tube, chain. I typically did not disassemble the drive sprockets and such, only what I needed to do to clean and lubricate the most actively moving parts. I can do an adequate job keeping the spokes on a wheel in tune. I'm no super bike mechanic or bike-tech detail expert, but I'm probably better than average, and know enough about bicycles to more than get by.

If you made it this far, go get a cookie, you earned it.

If you are a fairly inexperienced rider, I urge you to spend some time on the i-Net and learn about bikes and riding. Most importantly, learn what it takes to get a proper fit to your bike. A proper understanding of this will change your riding experience dramatically! Thisis one major advantage of buying a (good) bike at a shop with experienced mechanics and sales people. You can find really good info by web-searching phrases like: How to fit a bike for riding.

Good Luck on finding the right bike.

Be safe while riding!

(I had a motorcycle for a while. Best advice I got there was: "Ride like you are invisible". Same is true for bicycles IMHO.)

product_title: Yakima Products RidgeBack Hitch Bike Rack
review_headline: Great quality, easy to operate, solid bike rack
review_body:
Overall I kind of like this Bike rack - I have it installed into a standard 2inch towing hitch and the install was indeed very simple. I also purchased the HandCuff Bike lock and that was easy to fit in as well for some added security. I got the rack because we will need very soon to carry 4 bikes on short outings.

A lot of folks have commented on the positives of this bike rack (and there are many), so here are my list of stuff I found annoying:
- weight. This thing is heavy, but somehow the proportions feel a bit wrong. The tow hitch adapter is made to work with both 1.25 and 2inch hitch receivers, so the pipe going into the standard 2inch receiver is kind of on the thin side and sits awkwardly to one corner when mounted. It feels like the whole assembly is kind of too heavy for the small diameter bar connecting it to the hitch receiver.
- the bike mount posts are in fixed position. After putting on my bike, the second one needed another half inch distance away from the first bike to seat properly in the bike posts mounted on the rack. But since these don't move, I had to give up using position #2 and ended up using position #1, #3, and #4 for our three large bikes. This is kind of a bummer because when the toddler will graduate to a bike that no longer fits inside the car I will have to look for another "4 bike" rack which can actually accommodate 4 bikes.
- the way the straps are positioned and work, they require the bike seats to be turned about 45 degrees from their normal straight position. This required for me to get quick release bike seat clamps for the kids bikes as well, so that was an added expense I did not anticipate (If you ever hated your life while resetting a kids seat using the hex screw then you will know why a quick release clamp is a must here)
- the rack arms are quite widely spaced, so I had to purchase/use a bike top tube post because the arms were too wide by about an inch. Bummer.

I found the install and uninstall to be very straightforward and the operation of the bike rack to be quite pleasant and reassuring when loaded up with bikes. I really wish there would be a way to glide the bike mounting posts to achieve some custom spacing.raightforward and the operation of the bike rack to be quite pleasant and reassuring when loaded up with bikes. I really wish there would be a way to glide the bike mounting posts to achieve some custom spacing.

product_title: Fjallraven Men's Ovik Trousers
review_headline: Great pants! But what if your size is US30?
review_body:
I've owned the pants for about a month and have worn them for a week straight and I am really happy with them. I love the material. It is very light weight but also seems really wind resistance so it keeps out the cold. The large lower snap pocket on the right leg works great for my small moleskin notebook but the snap pocket on the left leg is too small to hold any of the newer smart phones. The pant legs are slim but not tight which is a bonus for me as I often have a hard time finding pants that are not too baggy.

If I had to come up with a negative I would say it is the lack of sizing options. The 44 seems to equate to a US 29 while the 46 equals a US 31. I am usually a US 30 so I had to try both. The 44 seemed to fit better. It was snug but not tight whereas the 46 was just a bit too big. If you are normally a US30 and like your pants a bit on the looser side I would recommend going with the 46. Also, while not necessarily a negative, the pants came in an unfinished length so I had to take them in to be hemmed. If you are handy with a sewing machine or a needle and thread you could probably do it yourself otherwise, factor the additional cost of alteration into your purchase. I would definitely buy another pair.

review_headline: Excellent boots, reccomend to US size 12 and lower
review_body: Just recieved these yesterday, and ive used them twice, once around the yard, and the other time for about 2 hours over the roughest terrain around. Both were incredible. The little thing that flips up helps a lot on slopes and hills, as it gives you more traction and keeps your ankles from over-bending. The amount of traction and flotation are awesome, i only give 4 stars because the bindings weren't large enough to fit my normal snowshoes, so i had to wear high-cut hiking shoes. Even though this probably made it a more comfortable, lighter, easier hike, i still would have liked my knee-high boots with built in gaiters. The bindings are extremely comfortable, yet still fit on the boot and hold your foot in with no wiggling. The platform stays down, and all the snow it picked up (though this was very little) Fell right through the holes leaving nothing on top. Overall, these shoes are excellent and i would highly reccomend them to anybody looking for a nice pair of snowshoes whose feet are size 12 and lower. I purchased the green and grey pair, both because they were cheaper and because they have better visibility (in case i need rescue or i go on a hike during hunting season.)

product_title: Profile Design Bottle Cage Stryke
review_headline: 36g Cage + 38g 1L SmartWater bottle for a full L of H2O held perfectly in place without popping the re-used bottled water bottle
review_body:
I give 5 stars even though I've had two of these break because that's been after years of use in both cases and a lot of bottle grabbing so I still think they are 5 stars based on the price, low weight, and perfect fit for 'Smart Water' water bottles which hold 1L of water and themselves only weigh 38g..

These cages weigh about 36g, which isn't bad. They fit a regular style water bottle well - holding it very firmly in place - but the real 5 stars is their fit of the 1L bottles.

That is what makes them a real 5 star item for me. Specifically, they fit perfectly the water bottles from the 'Smart Water' company which sells bottled water. I buy a 1L SmartWater bottle and then re-use it for either tap water or tap water mixed with electrolytes. It give me a full liter of water, which is much more than most standard bike bottle AND the SmartWater bottle weighs next to nothing. I've also gotten a nipple/pull style cap which screws onto the SmartWater bottle (from a different bottle water company's water bottle). Just get the one 1L bottle of bottled water, and then refill it. This bottle cage and those water bottles are an absolute perfect combination.

Other standard bottle cages can eventually pop the 1L bottle or don't hold it in place well. I have yet to find a 1L bottle that is as light as this one from the bottle water company, and this pairing of cage and bottle is excellent.

product_title: Mountain House Scrambled Eggs with Bacon
review_headline: Not Your Fathers Dehydrated Meal....Much Tastier, But A Small Breakfast Indeed...
review_body:
Being a hiker and camper from way back, something like this is nothing new to me. I have made many one pot meals over an open fire using dried tomato powder, dehydrated onion, celery, peppers, and many others...Believe it or not they are remembered as some of the best meals I have ever had. However when it came to breakfast, I always preferred the real thing. Real bacon, sausage, eggs, when I could manage it anyway. The bagged, dehydrated breakfasts and other meals could be pretty bad back then. They have actually come a long way with this Mountain House breakfast that taste much better than the ones I remember. I will even go as far as to say I thoroughly enjoyed it. Before I tried it I read some of the other reviews about the water that is called for and totally agree...Use half what they recommend. The full amount that is on the package is way too much and it comes out like an egg soup that really spoils it. About the only complaint I have with this is its being so little of it. There is less than 3 oz of meal here and its more like a snack than a breakfast. I could have definitely eaten double the amount...

Although the taste and texture of this to me was very good, this is the type of product that there will always be a core populace that will think it's just terrible. If you have never tried a dehydrated dinner before, I suggest this is no time to be adventuresome. The chances are generous that you will hate it. For the rest of us that are used to this type of meal, or, remember the ones of the past, I think you will be quite satisfied with this and its flavor. Like all dehydrated meals, its a little expensive for what you get, Which again, isn't much). But for a breakfast on the trail that can be stored near forever, it's not that bad at all, and I recommended it..: )

product_title: Columbia Sportswear All-Day Cruiser Backpack
review_body:
This is a great choice for a compact backpack. It has a very minimalist design and is lightweight. The canvas seems pretty tough - I just treated the bag to a month long tour of the western Balkans and it's come home with me looking pretty much like it's still brand new. I love that it is not flashy, and that the one inner pocket is hidden under the flap so it's easy to find small things that can be placed in it, yet is out of view from any potential pickpockets looking for an easy target. Or more likely, me forgetting to zip the pocket and everything falling out.

The closure is draw string, and then the front flap has two snaps - they are not magnetic, so it isn't a super quick pack up. The only things I'd change would be to add a stopper to the draw strings, to clamp it in place when it's pulled shut, and to make the snaps magnetic (hence the minus 1 star rating). Otherwise, I think it's a winner.

review_headline: Great light but prefer the S10R
review_body:
Great light, have this and the S10R. I sorta prefer carrying around the S10R more because of the smaller size. Also liked the reversible clip on the S10R so I can attach it to a ball cap. I know the S30R is a little wider but on a whim I took the pocket clip from the S10R and put it on the S30R. A little tight but it fits, removing it took a little bit of finger grip power, but the clip didn't seem bent out or stretched out, keep in mind I only had it on for a minute. Put the clip back on the S10R, still fits correctly without any looseness. I wish olight would have put that circular gap for the pocket clip on the other side also right below anti roll/power button area for the S30R, so it's own clip can be reversible, ala zebra light sc600 mkII.

The magnet for the S30R can only hold it vertically, cannot hold it sideways (another reason why I like the S10R a little more).

I read from selfbuilt's video review that he didn't recommend using the base charger for the S30R for any of the other Olight R batons, because S30R's is 750mah while the others were 500. I've charged my S10R on the 750 base with no issues so far. And both of my base chargers have worked with no issues so far, I know there were complaints about them.

product_title: Vargo Titanium Water Bottle with Titanium Lid
review_headline: If lightness is your first and only concern, this bottle is great.
review_body:
The bottle is fairly well made, with a few exceptions. The first is the thickness, or thinness rather, of the titanium used. Despite being made from titanium, the bottle feels cheap and can be dented with your bare hands. Vargo's parsimonious use of material is both unnecessary and highly unfortunate. Instead of a lightweight and robust bottle, we have a featherweight and flimsy bottle. I sincerely doubt many people would have been bothered by or would have even noticed an additional ounce or two, had the bottle walls been 50% thicker. Yet, that additional thickness would have made a world of difference as far as durability and perceived quality are concerned.

The two primary reasons for selecting titanium in this application are its non-reactive/non-toxic properties, and its strength. Lightness is merely the icing on the cake. The only reason I can think of for using such thin material to construct this bottle is to save on the cost of materials. But titanium is not platinum and this level of cost cutting seems excessive to the extent of greediness.

The second issue with the bottle is the lid. It was a good idea to create a bottle entirely out of titanium, thus eliminating any contact with materials that may leach harmful substances into liquids stored within. However, the execution of this idea leaves much to be desired. The lid is not only noisy, but is easily cross-threaded. Worse yet, the friction from the metal on metal contact of the threads generates fine particulate matter. In an attempt to "break in" the lid and reduce the noise involved with tightening and loosening it, I applied some coconut oil to the threads and repeatedly tightened and loosened it. When I cleaned off the oil, the paper towel came away gray with titanium dust. It may be safe to drink, but that doesn't mean I want such dust contaminating my water. As suggested by another reviewer, a clamp down lid would be a much better design. This would eliminate both thenoise and the metal particles that result from a threaded lid.

If these design shortcomings were rectified, I would gladly pay $100 or more for such a bottle. As it stands, $40 would be a more appropriate price for this bottle.

product_title: Abus Mini Round Shackle U Lock, 5.5"/15mm
review_headline: The little red (or yellow) U-lock that could!
review_body:
For the price and level of security, this lock is hard to beat. Double-bolted and light as well. I purchased 3 of these. 1 locks my 1up bike rack to the hitch. 1 I use for my bike and 1 as a spare. I tried to use it against my 29er but the lock is just too small to lock through wheel and stays. It can be done but I did not want to have to think about how to lock the mountain bike every time. I ended up using another Abus lock - Abus Bordo Granit-X -
( http://amzn.com/B005VMO4CW) to lock up the mountain bike. The Abus Mini is perfect for my road bike. Wheels, frames and stays are thin enough that I can lock my road bike's rear wheel and frame or stay in the u-lock without having to resort to using the Sheldon technique.

I solved the problem of lack of mounting unit by using the Kryptonite TransFit FlexFrame Bracket (http://www.amazon.com/Kryptonite-Transfit-FlexFrame-U-Bracket/dp/B00J4044ZO). The bracket kit comes with 13mm and 16mm shackle adapters. The Abus mini has a 14mm shackle diameter. I had to remove part of the rubber cover of the Abus mini so I can fit the 16mm Kryptonite shackle mount adapter. Just cut enough of the rubber cover to make room for the shackle adapter and the u-lock shackle should still have the necessary rubber cover that should protect the bike finish. A little bit of fitting and the Abus mini is now mounted to my bike using the FlexFrame bracket. (Pictures TBD)

product_title: Black Men's Ski Gloves - Size Medium - XXL
review_headline: It really depends on your use
review_body:
If you're looking for legitimate ski gloves DO NOT BUY these. There is hardly any grip on the palm and they don't seem well suited for skiing (as someone who skis). If, however, you are going out with your friends once or maybe twice in a season, they'd probably be just 'fine.' I would recommend getting actual ski gloves if you think you'll be going out any more than that.

I bought them for my boyfriend to clear off the car in the morning, shovel, etc. They were KINDA OKAY for those things. The Velcro strap doesn't go all the way around and can come off with anything more vigorous than shoveling (the velcro undid itself while driving). There is a gap in between the lining and the outer part of the glove. The gap is about the width of a woman's finger and is filled with fluff. So, you might not get the best grip or be as dexterous as you'd like... and it's just...annoying.

They are warm, a bit bigger than expected, and a tad bulky but comfortable.

He would give them a four, I'd give them a 3.... so, 3.5/5. Good for it's purpose but it depends on your purpose. Not a bad price (especially if you have Prime shipping), and I figure they will last a couple seasons with his type of use.

product_title: Infuser Water Bottle Sport Flip-top BPA-Free Tritan 25 Oz (Multiple Infused Water Color Options)
review_headline: Love it so much, it's practically attached to my hand!
review_body:
I received my water bottle a couple of weeks ago but wanted to wait until I got a few uses out of it before writing a detailed and accurate review for my fellow Amazonians. I have never had an infuser water bottle before so I really don't have anything else to compare this to, but this bottle has been INCREDIBLE for what I needed it for!! When choosing between this water bottle and the other infuser water bottles Amazon has to offer, the thing that really won me over about this bottle (aside from the overwhelming amount of 5 star reviews) is that it was one of the only bottles that had a flip-top spout. This is SUPER important to me because it makes it such a hassle to have to twist off the cap every time you want to have a sip of water. There's also a lock on the cap that keeps the flip-top from just springing open on accident. This feature alone takes the cake for me, especially since I always have my bottle in one of my carry-on bags.

To better understand why I needed this water bottle, you should know that I am a flight attendant. Flying as much as I do, it's super important to stay hydrated and if I'm being honest, I kind of suck at making sure I drink enough water throughout the day, especially when I'm flying. I ordered this water bottle because I LOVE fruit infused water and find I drink TONS of it when it's available to me. This bottle holds about 20 ounces of water (even with a decent amount of fruit inside), and probably about 18 ounces if you add ice cubes to your water. There are two types of filters in this bottle, one you can see in the picture (which I originally thought was what you put the fruit in, but found you don't need to), and the other is at the top of that filter, which has tiny holes that allows almost NOTHING to get through. Strawberry infused water is my absolute favorite and for the first time in forever I ended up drinking and filling up this bottle 8 TIMES the other day. That's 160 ounces of water in one day (which for me is a LOT). I did it without even thinking about it, I would aimlessly just drink this water throughout the day instead of snacking on junk food. I couldn't believe how full I felt for most of the day between meals just from drinking a lot of water. AND to top it off, the strawberry seeds never got through the infuser filter! Not a single one! And surprisingly, I never had to change out the fruit throughout the day, I would just refill the bottle with water, let the water sit for about 5-10 minutes to allow the fruit to infuse the water and I was good to go until I had to fill it up with water again! On the Amazon page it says, "With your infusion water bottles you can re-fill it 3 to 4 times with the same fruit. After 12 hours we suggest you refresh the fruit in the bottle," but for me so far the fruit (no matter what kind) has lasted up to almost 20 hours and I've filled it up to 8 times before I really need to refresh the fruit. I really enjoy being able to taste the fruit in my water so I put a decent sized handful of fruit in my bottle. If you like having a lot of fruit in your bottle like me, I suggest you put the fruit in your empty bottle first, fill it with water almost to the top, then put the cap with the filter on. If you only want a little bit of fruit in your water and not be able to taste it too much, just twist off the filter and add your fruit inside of it and it should be able to hold just enough for your liking.

HINT: I suggest peeling any fruits with rinds (so basically any citrus fruits) before you put it in your water. The rinds will make your water taste bitter. I first cut my oranges, lemons, and limes into thin (but not too thin) slices, then take the peel off and discard it, and mash the fruit up a little bit with my fingers before putting it in the bottle. This may seem like too much work if you're in a hurry, but it really only takes a couple of minutes and you're seriously good to go for the rest of the day!

Oh, and one last feature I forgot to mention above, it does come with a little "strap" so you can hook it onto your bike or backpack, but I've had no real use for it, and unfortunately it doesn't come off (unless maybe you found something heavy duty to cut it off). That is literally the ONLY thing I don't absolutely love about this water bottle. I've attached some pictures of my water bottle filled with strawberries, and a shot of the filter. I bought the blue color, and I love this water bottle so much that I bought one in orange for my mom! All of my co-workers have been jealous of my water bottle and ask me where I bought it. Hope this review is helpful to some of you trying to choose the right infuser water bottle for your lifestyle. review_headline: simple, high quality, real world tool that gives the best value per dollar spent than any other light I have owned or used
review_body: 3 years and going strong ! BOTH my bc20s look like bobofets helmet with dings scratches and considerable wear  ...distressed finish is all the rage these days right?  Hands down of all the dozens of high end edc tactical and working lights this is my all around favorite due to the no nonsense "user interface"  how often do you really need 800 lumens? almost never..300 is perfect for when you need it bright folks, 20 is a very useable amount and a perfect low setting..simple one button...ON..OFF and twist the head left right for hi and low . WOW ! no stupid sos strobe morse freakin code crap to cycle thru or even deal with at all ..... if I find myself at sea stranded in a life raft or lost for days in the wilderness and I hear a plane searching overhead Im pretty confident I will muster the energy and coordinaton it takes to simply press that tailcap button momentarily and make it flash ...also waving it side to side serves the same purpose to someone looking for a signal so theres your sos mode.. if you need that type nerd gimmicky crap feature your probably just itching to waste your money on something else anyway and this wasnt even on your shortlist. If you must have a strobe feature your obviously on a swat team and get issued something else anyway or simply wish to annoy people at the range or have to have that overrated feature to brag about to buddies or to fill that void in your life until the next cool gadget catches your eye..SERIOUSLY you dont need that first off and second is it really worth the extra cost for that type of feature...  weapons mounted application ? YUP got that covered  I have one of these on the homes go too long gun  .. a simple ak 74 variant built on a polish tantal kit .Its mounted using a very simple shotgun mag "tube clamp" type mount that cost about 15 bucks and is extremely simple and robust, your mounting will vary depending on gun but its the same diameter as most of the tactical lights out there so that shouldnbe an issue. its positioned on the left side right off the bulgarian type gas block , where my left thumb can rest right on the switch naturally .. its the freakin perfect location , not a huge protrusion or snag creator and doesnt require remote switch with wires hanging all over and even with sustained fire never heats up the light ...its held up to thousands of rounds and plenty of run and gun type practical rifle matches and even a few low light range sessions without a hiccup .

product_title: Attwood Marine Attwood Kayak Hoist System - Black
review_body: Gave it 4 stars only because we had to perform some modifications.  Our garage ceiling is not that high, so we had to remove the J hooks to raise the kayaks high enough and come up with an alternative way to hook them to the hoist.  Otherwise, it appears to be a very good product.  We were perplexed by some of the comments that the kayaks come crashing down.  We would never hang anything heavy without backup strapping in place.  We can't imagine any product being able to support that kind of weight on its own and still be able to easily release it to lower the kayaks.  Simply put, once the kayaks are hoisted, we have anchored ropes which we attach to the front and back handle hooks.  Problem solved.  Upon releasing, however, sometimes we do need to climb a ladder to get each hoist to let go of its grip. product_title: OverBoard Waterproof Pro-Sport Backpack
review_headline: and pretty much every other activity that could involve water and ...
review_body: Why should you buy this bag over other dry backpacks? For one, it is 100% waterproof and has an IP code of IP66 (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_Code). What's this you ask? Its a measure the degree of protection provided against intrusion (body parts such as hands and fingers), dust, accidental contact, and water by mechanical casings and electrical enclosures. Most bag companies such as Ortlieb make their waterproof bags with only a IP64 rating. Second, the bag is made with fully welded seamless construction of PVC coated 600D nylon, most other companies only use 400-500D. Another reason you should get this bag over other dry backpacks is because of it's versatility. I use this bag for sailing, biking, canoeing, and pretty much every other activity that could involve water and rain. The full mesh back is great for people who sweat a lot or who want to use the bag for activities where you might sweat a lot. In terms of sizing, I would recommend the 20L for smaller people, as it sits higher on your back, and the 30L for people with longer torsos because it sits a bit lower on your back. Overall I recommend the 30L over the 20L because if you don't use all the space in the 30L bag you can always compress it down to a smaller size.

I have had many flashlights in the past from surefire flashlights to El cheapo off the slow boat from China. All of said flashlights have lasted MUCH LONGER than 5 minutes!!!
Here's the breakdown of what happened. Just recieved the Nite core flashlight today. Got home from work, eagerly opened the package, loaded the fully charged nite core 3400mAh battery and began to test the flashlight out. High, low, strobe, sos and infinite adjustability all worked perfectly and really bright, until I dropped it from a 3 ft height off the kitchen island right on its side. Now, it doesn't work. I've even tried using other 18650 batteries I had. Still doesn't work! My cheap $30 flashlight has taken many hits and still works!!!
Maybe this is a fluke exception, but I can not trust my life with Nite core.

product_title: Helly Hansen Women's Squamish CIS (3-in-1) Rain Jacket
review_body:
*POST-SKI TRIP UPDATE* My wife wore this jacket for a week of skiing in Utah. Granted - 4 of 6 days were in the the high 30's and sunny, but this jacket worked flawlessly, and even garnered compliments from a hired pro and ski-shop workers and friends. She also found that the hood is indeed roomy enough to fit over a helmet when adjusted properly, which is not so useful on warm days but is always nice on a windy chairlift. On the colder days this was a excellent outer layer, and if it had been even warmer she would've gone without the liner so this is a no-brainer for a ski trip.

This is a very nice looking jacket if you like the dark-purple color. The shell material still has a softness to it that belies it's weatherproofness. It almost feels like suede, and is very nice to touch. In fact, despite it's purplishness this jacket is quite stylish, and my wife got compliments left and right on it here in New York City's latest wintry mix of snow and ice and rain.

She is wearing it for the winter weather now, but really we got it for an upcoming ski-trip. We've worn Helly/Hansen jackets for skiing for years and were happy to take them up on a free upgrade. Unfortunately, after wearing it around for a while I think we are a little disappointed... not in the construction or the style, but the I am afraid the design leaves a few things to be desired for real winter sports.

Basically, this is a 3-in-1 jacket - the shell and the lining can either be worn separately or zipped together to make an insulated winter jacket. That part all looks and works great. It's reasonably warm, and the windproofing and weatherproofing seem top-notch. The outer pockets are lightly lined and officially qualify as \\"hand-warmer\\" pockets, but they could be cozier. The hood can be operated one-handed and the zippers all have nice long pull-tabs for gloved operation. Cuffs and the waist are all easily adjustable and cinchable, and zipping in the liner is pretty straighforward, and once it's in it feels like it was built in.

All that sounds great, right? The problems are really that there seem to be some things left out that would make this a better winter-sport jacket. Mainly, the lack of inner pockets and a detachable powder-skirt are making my wife less than thrilled about wearing this on the mountain. There's nowhere to stuff your gloves (not to mention goggles). Even if you leave those out, there is no great place inside the coat to stuff a phone and a wallet.

That being said, the coat is versatile and it's nice you can wear it in different configurations and will work in a range of conditions. And it will definitely keep you dry and pretty warm.

It also runs a little small - we'd usually get a small but the medium fit better., and once it's in it feels like it was built in. All that sounds great, right?
